slides.title: The USA PATRIOT Act & OFAC
slides.description:
In this course we will review the USA PATRIOT Act and OFAC

With over 15 government agencies and over 150 Federal laws from Gramm-Leach-Bliley, EPA, Patriot Act, Red Flag, OSHA, and EEOC to name just a few, compliance has never been more complicated or necessary.

Automotive Compliance Consultants works with dealerships to understand the compliance and regulatory maze that exists in all aspects of the dealership environment. With offices from coast-to-coast we help hundreds of dealerships with these programs from top 100 to small single point dealerships.

slides.title: The Patriot Act
slides.description:
The USA PATRIOT Act is short for “The Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001”. Congress enacted the USA PATRIOT Act to deter terrorist acts and money laundering activities, and to enhance law enforcement investigatory tools.

Fines for failing to comply with the Patriot Act, and its regulations can result in significant fines ranging from $100 to $500,000 for negligent violations

slides.title: PATRIOT Act Requirements
slides.description:
The PATRIOT Act applies to dealership operations. A goal of the Act is to prevent money from terrorist and illegal activities from being laundered through legitimate businesses. Compliance with the Act requires a dealership to:

“Know their customers,” (OFAC) identify and report suspicious financial transactions, maintain reports, and respond to inquiries from government officials.

Establish an anti-money laundering program

Designate a compliance officer

Maintain ongoing employee training programs

Report cash transactions of $10,000 or more (FinCEN)

slides.title: FinCEN Cash Reporting
slides.description:
The Patriot Act gave theFinancial Crimes Enforcement Network (“FinCEN”)additional responsibilities and authorities, and established the organization as a bureau within the Department of the Treasury (“Treasury”). The mission of FinCEN is to support law enforcement investigative efforts and foster interagency and global cooperation against domestic and international financial crimes.

Dealerships are required to file reports with FinCEN for any transaction where $10,000 or greater in cash is received. The dealership must file IRS form 8300 within fifteen (15) days after the date more than $10,000 is received.

slides.title: Cash Transaction(s)
slides.description:
The receipt of $10,000 or greater in cash can occur in one transaction or in two or more related transactions, and triggers FinCEN reporting.

Cash transactions of $10,000 or greater can occur:

In a lump sum single transaction;

Two or more payments totaling over $10,000; or

payments received as part of a single transaction (or two or more related transactions) that cause the total cash received within a 12 month period to total over $10,000.

slides.title: What Constitutes Cash?
slides.description:
Payments considered to be in cash are:

Any currency

Money orders, cashier’s check, certified bank check, or traveler’s check in an amount LESS than $10,000 (Note: when these instruments are issued for more than $10,000 they are not treated as cash as the institution issuing the instrument has already dealt with any FinCen reporting). There are, however, exceptions to when these instruments issued for less than $10,000 will not constitute cash.

slides.title: Payments NOT Considered Cash
slides.description:
Cash does NOT include:

Proceeds from a loan

Personal Check

Business Check

Funds wired from a Bank

Certified business or personal check

Financial institution wire transfers

Traveler’s checks, cashier’s checks, certified bank checks, and money orders are not deemed cash when they are in an amount in excess of $10,000 or regardless of the amount:

They are proceeds from a bank or credit union loan

They are received on the payment of a promissory note or an installment contract, and

(i) promissory notes or installment contracts are customarily used in the ordinary course of business for retail sales; and

(ii) the total payments for the sale received on or before the 60th day after the sale are 50% or less of the purchase price.

slides.title: What is a “Transaction?”
slides.description:
FinCen reporting is required where cash of more than $10,000 is received in a single transaction, or in two or more “related transactions.” For a dealership a transaction is the sale of any goods or services.

Related Transactions

Transactions are related if they occur within a 24-hour period. Transactions are also related even if they are more than 24 hours apart ifyou know, or have reason to know,that each is one of a series of connected transactions. For example, items or services negotiated during the original purchase are related to the original purchase.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.description:
A customer purchased a vehicle for $9,000 cash. Within the next 12 months, the customer paid the dealership additional cash of $1,500 for a repair to the vehicle's transmission, accessories and a customized paint job, etc. Should a Form 8300 be filed?

Answer:No, unless the dealer knew or had reason to know the sale of the vehicle and the subsequent transactions were a series of connected transactions.

The answer would be yes, if the dealer and the customer agreed, as a condition of the sale of the vehicle, that the customer would be obligated to buy an additional $1,500 of goods or services.

The answer would also be yes if the transactions described above occurred within a 24 hour period, even if the repair and accessories were an after thought, and not contemplated at the time of the initial sale.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.description:
A customer makes weekly payments in cash to the dealership as a lease or loan payment on a vehicle. During a 12-month period, these payments total more than $10,000. Are these payments considered related transactions and is the dealership required to file a Form 8300?

Answer:Yes, the weekly lease or loan payments constitute payments on the same transaction (the leasing or purchase of the vehicle). The dealership is required to file Form 8300 each time the total amount of cash payments exceed $10,000. If the customer paid the dealer in excess of $30,000, but less than $40,000 in cash over the full term of the loan/lease, the dealer would have filed three (3) Form 8300s.

slides.title: Example 3
slides.description:
Do payments in excess of $10,000 in cash paid to a body shop need to be reported?

Answer:Yes. Cash, in the form of currency, received in excess of $10,000 must be reported.

Note:A service is not a consumer durable so the expanded definition of cash (cashier’s checks, money orders etc. under $10,000) does not apply to payments for services. The body shop would file an 8300 in this case as cash was used to pay.

slides.title: Example 4
slides.description:
A dealership receives greater than $10,000 in cash on day one for the sale of a vehicle. On day three, the deal is cancelled due to an inability to finance the deal. The dealership returns the cash. Is a Form 8300 required?

Answer:Yes. Once the dealership receives cash exceeding $10,000, a Form 8300 must be filed. The deal not going through may in fact be an attempt to launder illegal funds. If $10,000 or less was received by the dealer and the deal was cancelled, the dealer may voluntarily file a Form 8300 if the transaction appears suspicious.

slides.title: Example 5
slides.description:
Dealer sells a car for $12,000. The buyer pays $8,000 in cash and puts the rest on a credit card. Is a Form 8300 required?

Answer:No. Payments made by credit or debit card are not considered cash payments. Therefore, no FinCen report is required unless the transaction appears suspicious.

slides.title: FinCEN and 8300 Reporting Requirements
slides.description:
A dealership must file Form 8300 within 15 days after the date the cash was received on any transaction that requires reporting.

Each time the payments aggregate in excess of $10,000 on what would be considered a related transaction, the dealership must file another Form 8300 within 15 days of the payment that causes the additional payments to total more than $10,000.

Customer Report

A dealership must notify its customer that a Form 8300 was filed regarding the cash transaction with the customer.

The notice must be written or electronic statement to each person named on the Form 8300.

The notice must be given on or before January 31 of the year following the calendar year in which the cash is received.

The statement must show the name, telephone number, and address of the information contact for the dealership, the aggregate amount of reportable cash received, and that the information was furnished to the IRS.

slides.title: Penalties
slides.description:
The penalties for filing late or incorrect reports, or failing to file reports on cash transactions over $10,000 are significant.

• There are civil penalties for failure to file a correct Form 8300 by its due date and for failure to provide a statement as required. Civil penalties range from $100 per return to $500,000. For businesses with gross receipts exceeding $5 million the maximum can be increased to $1.5 million per year.

A minimum penalty of $25,0000 may apply for intentional disregard of the filing requirements.

Criminal penalties may apply in the case of willful filing of false or fraudulent Forms 8300 which may result in imprisonment of up to 5 years or fines of up to $25,000 for individuals and $100,000 for corporations, or both.

slides.title: PFinCEN Investigation and Information Requests
slides.description:
The Treasury has issued “Special Information Sharing Procedures to Deter Money Laundering and Terrorist Activity.” If law enforcement officials have “credible evidence” of a suspect’s involvement in money laundering or terrorism activities, they may send a request to banks and other financial institutions (including dealers), requiring the recipient to search its records for account or transaction information concerning the individual or entity named in the request, and to provide such information to the requesting law enforcement official. Dealerships are required to respond “expeditiously” to any such request.

Dealers must maintain adequate procedures to protect the security and confidentiality of requests from FinCEN for information. This requirement is deemed satisfied if a dealer applies to this information the same procedures it has established to comply with section 501 of the Gramm Leach Bliley Act (15 U.S.C. § 6801) and the Federal Trade Commission’s implementing regulation (16 CFR Part 314) pertaining to the protection of customers’ nonpublic personal information.

slides.title: OFAC
slides.description:
"OFAC" stands for the Office of Foreign Assets Control, an office of the Department of the Treasury located in Washington D.C. A division of the Department of the Treasury, OFAC administers and enforces economic and trade sanctions based on U.S. foreign policy and national security goals against targeted foreign countries and regimes, terrorists, international narcotics traffickers, those engaged in activities related to the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and other threats to the national security, foreign policy or economy of the United States.

Presidential Executive Order 13224, signed by President George W. Bush on September 24, 2001, prohibits persons from transacting business with any person listed on the “SDN List.” Specifically, it provides that “all property and interest in property of the [specially designated nationals] that are in the United States, or that hereafter come within the United States, or hereafter come within the possession or control of United States persons are blocked.” Many dealers are unaware that OFAC applies to them, and requires them to check customer names against the SDN list in every transaction.

Transacting business with persons and entities identified on the SDN list is prohibited. OFAC applies to all transactions, regardless of the amount or whether they are cash or credit.

slides.title: What is the “SDN” list?
slides.description:
OFAC has designated individuals, banks, companies, and other entities who are considered a threat to national security, or who participate in activities that are against U.S. foreign policy. Their names are placed on the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (SDN list), which can be found on OFAC’s website (www.treas.gov/ofac).

Dealership customer names must be checked against the SDN list prior to completing the sale.

slides.title: I Ran a Name and Got a Match. Now what?
slides.description:
If you have checked a name manually or by using software and find a match, you should do a little more research.

Is it an exact name match, or very close?

Is your customer located in the same general area as the SDN?

If neither of the above apply it may be a "false hit."

If, however, there are many similarities, contact OFAC's "hotline" at 1-800-540-6322 for verification.

Unless you have an exact match or are otherwise privy to information indicating that the hit is a target, it is recommended that you not actually block a transaction without discussing the matter with OFAC.

slides.title: Blocked Transactions
slides.description:
In the case of an exact match or OFAC verifies a match, the dealership must then block the transaction.

Any time a transaction is blocked a report must be filed with OFAC within 10 business days of blocking the transaction. The written report to OFAC must include the name of the blocked person, property, location of property, account information, estimated value, date blocked, a photocopy of the payment, and the business name and phone contact for the dealership representative making the report.

Records for all blocked OFAC transactions must be maintained for five (5) years.

slides.title: Failure to Comply
slides.description:
The OFAC has the authority to impose substantial fines for violations. General guidelines for violations are as follows:

$1,000 for a transaction valued at less than $1,000

$10,000 for a transaction valued at $1,000 or more but less than $10,000;

$25,000 for a transaction valued at $10,000 or more but less than $25,000;

$50,000 for a transaction valued at $25,000 or more but less than $50,000;

$100,000 for a transaction valued at $50,000 or more but less than $100,000;

$170,000 for a transaction valued at $100,000 or more but less than $170,000; and $250,000 for a transaction valued at $170,000 or more

In addition to civil penalties, criminal penalties for willful violations can include fines ranging up to $20 million and imprisonment of up to 30 years.

Note the following Agency statement:

A person who processes an unauthorized transaction involving an SDN has violated U.S. law and may be subject to an enforcement action. Generally speaking, however, if (i) the only sanctions reference in the transaction is a weak AKA, (ii) the person involved in the processing had no other reason to know that the transaction involved an SDN or was otherwise in violation of U.S. law, and (iii) the person maintains a rigorous risk-based compliance program, OFAC will not issue a civil penalty against an individual or entity for processing such a transaction.
